nameStory: The variable wrinkle-lichen gets its name from the distinctive wrinkled, bumpy surface that looks like crumpled paper or elephant skin. The 'variable' part refers to how different it can look depending on growing conditions - sometimes smooth, sometimes deeply furrowed, and changing color dramatically when wet versus dry.
description: Variable wrinkle-lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that forms irregular patches on tree bark, looking like gray-green leather that's been wadded up and smoothed out again. The surface has a characteristic wrinkled, bumpy texture with wavy ridges and valleys. It typically grows 2-4 inches across, though older specimens can spread much larger, and ranges from pale gray when dry to olive-green when moist.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The surface feels like soft, wrinkled leather with distinctive bumps and ridges that create a wavy, undulating pattern across the entire lichen

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms irregular, leafy patches that are loosely attached to bark with slightly upturned edges, like pieces of textured paper glued down at the center

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shifts from pale gray or whitish-gray when dry to olive-green or brownish-green when wet, with the color change happening within minutes of moisture

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on the bark of hardwood trees, especially maples and oaks, rarely on conifers or rocks

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: May have small, dark brown cup-shaped structures (apothecia) scattered across the surface, but these are uncommon in New England specimens

habitat: Variable wrinkle-lichen prefers the bark of mature hardwood trees in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, particularly favoring maples, oaks, and birches. It's most common at mid-elevations in areas with moderate air pollution levels, often found in suburban woodlands and parks rather than deep wilderness areas.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the olive-green wet coloration is easily visible. New growth edges may appear slightly brighter than older sections.
seasonality.summer: Often appears pale and grayish during dry spells, but transforms to green within minutes of summer thunderstorms. The wrinkled texture is most pronounced when dry.
seasonality.fall: Color changes are most dramatic during fall's wet weather, shifting between gray and green as moisture levels fluctuate with changing temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible and identifiable on bare tree bark, often appearing pale gray against dark bark. Snow contact briefly brings out green coloration.

funFact: Variable wrinkle-lichen can absorb up to 35 times its dry weight in water, causing it to completely change color from gray to green in less than 30 seconds - faster than a mood ring!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other gray foliose lichens like rock tripe, but variable wrinkle-lichen's distinctive bumpy, wrinkled surface texture sets it apart - think 'crumpled paper' versus the smoother surfaces of similar species. Remember: if it feels like wrinkled leather on tree bark, you've likely found your lichen.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'variable,' this lichen is actually quite consistent in its wrinkled appearance - the name refers more to its dramatic color changes with moisture rather than highly variable forms. It belongs to a small genus of wrinkle-lichens that were once grouped with other shield lichens until scientists recognized their unique characteristics.
compareHints: Variable wrinkle-lichen differs from its relatives by having the most pronounced wrinkled texture - fringed wrinkle-lichen has hair-like projections along edges, while trailrunner forms more elongated, strap-like lobes. Chestnut wrinkle-lichen has a distinctly brownish cast even when dry, whereas variable wrinkle-lichen is typically gray to whitish when dry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: **[Uncertain claim flag]** Compared to Variable Wrinkle-lichen, Fringed Wrinkle Lichen has much more prominent and consistently present fringe hairs along its edges.
Trailrunner differs from its cousin Fringed Wrinkle Lichen by having more pronounced cilia and typically narrower lobes.
